plot_extraction.response_text:
An elite retail salesman works a brutal Black Friday in a mall where consumer frenzy turns shoppers into violent, barely human creatures. Because he was bitten during a previous sale, he can understand their incoherent demands and uses this ability to achieve record sales while fending them off and witnessing numerous injuries and deaths. He hopes to win the store’s sales contest and give his unemployed mother an expensive parka as proof of his love.

A new employee, Duo, gains the same ability after being bitten but quits, unable to accept the suffering around him. He tells the salesman that a coat cannot prove his love and that his mother already knows he cares. Soon afterward, the salesman sacrifices the only parka in his mother’s size to satisfy a frenzied shopper and save his manager from being attacked. Though his prize is gone and the horror of the event is clear, he returns to his section, embraces his role, and welcomes another stampeding crowd with practiced enthusiasm.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story uses a first-person, present-tense perspective that locks the reader into the consciousness of a highly capable but emotionally constricted retail worker. The narrator’s voice is blunt, observant, competitive, and darkly funny. He treats grotesque violence as ordinary workplace inconvenience, while discussing sales targets, product specifications, shift coverage, and customer service with complete seriousness. This deadpan collision between retail language and horror creates the story’s central stylistic effect. The narration rarely announces moral judgments; instead, the absurdity and cruelty emerge through the narrator’s practical acceptance of them.

The prose is direct and largely built from short declarative sentences, fragments, and compact paragraphs. Abrupt constructions such as “His slobber hot” or “A sickle, half circle, my lucky Friday scar” give the voice a clipped, bodily immediacy. During crowd scenes, rapid lists and repeated verbs accelerate the pace: people “scream and hiss and claw and moan,” while products, sizes, and relationships arrive in compressed sequences. Longer sentences are used selectively for product descriptions, corporate language, or explanations of consumer desire. This contrast makes advertising copy and managerial jargon sound especially grotesque when placed beside crushed fingers, bites, corpses, and blood.

The diction mixes three main registers: colloquial speech, visceral horror, and commercial branding. Casual phrases such as “pretty good kid,” “that shit is sad,” and “greatest goddamn salesman” establish an unpolished working-class voice. Graphic physical details—foam, teeth, wounds, bodies, blood, trampled children—supply the horror. Against these sits a dense layer of fabricated brand names and retail terminology, including PoleFace™, SuperShell, SleekPack, Coalmeister, face-out racks, daily breakdowns, sales goals, commissions, and pallet jacks. The trademark symbol is an important satirical touch, suggesting that corporate ownership and branding remain meticulously protected even as human life becomes disposable.

Imagery is concrete, kinetic, and frequently animalistic. Shoppers howl, claw, stampede, hiss, bite, and foam at the mouth; crowds become waves, herds, or ravenous packs. Similes are vivid but accessible, such as fingers appearing “like worms through the grating” or the food-court smell masking death “like a muzzle on a rabid dog.” The store is transformed into a battlefield, slaughterhouse, and arena, yet it retains the recognizable furniture of ordinary retail. This literalization of consumer frenzy gives the speculative premise its force: familiar metaphors about bargain hunters becoming animals are made physically real.

Dialogue is terse and functional. Characters often speak in fragments, commands, product names, sizes, and slogans rather than complete sentences. The infected shoppers’ broken language compresses identity, need, shame, and family obligation into retail requests. The narrator’s supernatural ability to “speak Black Friday” allows him to translate these cries into fuller interior motives, often presented as fragmented streams of thought: the desire to be a good father, to fit in at work, to keep a family together, or to prove love through a purchase. This device adds pathos without softening the satire. Consumer hunger is monstrous, but it grows from recognizable emotional and economic pressures.

The humor is macabre, understated, and cumulative. Bodies are assigned a designated section; a child who may still be alive is nearly swept onto a pallet jack; corporate management describes mass death through phrases such as “customer care and interpersonal cohesiveness.” The narrator reads the mall’s bloody condition as evidence of “a great Black Friday.” These jokes are delivered without a comic pause, preserving the deadpan tone. Corporate euphemism is especially important: it sanitizes catastrophe and exposes an institutional worldview in which casualties matter less than sales performance.

Characterization is achieved through action, workplace hierarchy, and attitudes toward selling rather than extensive physical description. The narrator defines himself by competence. His pride in being the best salesman is genuine, and the story does not reduce him to a simple victim or villain. He is ruthless, vain, resilient, and capable of violence, but he also understands customers, protects coworkers, feeds a bereaved woman, and wants to give his mother an expensive coat. His emotional life has been translated into the same commodity logic that governs the shoppers: the coat is supposed to serve as proof of permanent love. Duo functions as a moral counterpoint because he develops the same supernatural understanding yet rejects the job’s demands. His statement that “the coat isn’t proof” briefly punctures the narrator’s sustaining belief.

The structure is mostly chronological, following the opening rush, the lull, the break, Duo’s departure, and the narrator’s return to the sales floor. Short retrospective passages about earlier Black Fridays deepen the narrator’s identity and reveal how thoroughly the event has shaped him. These flashbacks are attached to practical triggers such as a scar, a sales contest, food, or commission, so they do not interrupt the momentum. Repeated references to his first, second, third, and fourth Black Fridays create a ritualistic progression and suggest initiation into a recurring system of violence.

Pacing alternates between frantic set pieces and quieter moments of emotional exposure. The opening begins at maximum tension, with the gate about to rise and the crowd already behaving like predators. The first sales sequence is fast, crowded, and physically chaotic. The food-court scene slows the narrative, allowing grief, hunger, poverty, and family breakdown to become more visible. The final movement accelerates again as the narrator sacrifices the coat, returns to his section, and faces another stampede. This rhythm keeps the story energetic while ensuring that its social critique is not lost inside the spectacle.

The setting is established through selective, recognizable details rather than extensive exposition. The mall’s escalators, food court, Christmas music, chain restaurants, registers, stockrooms, racks, and motivational corporate language make the surreal world feel plausible. Exposition about “the Friday Black” is embedded casually in the narrator’s workplace knowledge. Because he regards the phenomenon as normal, the story avoids lengthy explanation and lets the reader infer the rules: violence is expected, bites transmit understanding, casualties are routine, and management accommodates the disaster rather than preventing it.

Tonally, the story combines splatter horror, dystopian satire, workplace comedy, and muted tragedy. Its surface is energetic and outrageous, but beneath that surface lies an atmosphere of economic despair. Shoppers are driven by scarcity, status anxiety, parental guilt, loneliness, and the belief that affection must be materialized through products. Employees remain at risk for low wages and uncertain rewards. The narrator’s family has been damaged by “lean living,” while the mall offers commodities as substitutes for intimacy and self-worth. Christmas is described as the mall’s god, reinforcing the fusion of religious devotion, consumer ritual, and sacrifice.

Repetition provides thematic and rhythmic cohesion. Product names, family roles, sales figures, the phrase “Black Friday,” and the language of strength and weakness recur throughout. The narrator repeatedly returns to the idea that exceptional sales ability gives him value. Likewise, gestures of care repeatedly take commercial form: fathers buy jackets, families seek matching coats, and the narrator plans to demonstrate love through a prize. The closing customer-service question echoes the opening command and completes the cycle. After sacrifice, disillusionment, and mass death, the narrator resumes his professional role with a smile.

Overall, the style is fast, visceral, sardonic, and voice-driven. Its defining technique is the seamless treatment of supernatural carnage as standard retail procedure. The strongest emotional moments remain restrained rather than sentimental, usually appearing through plain statements, awkward silences, or failed attempts at connection. The ending preserves the narrator’s ambiguity: his final smile may signal resilience, surrender, pride, indoctrination, or all four at once.

generation.response_text:
The gate shakes in its track.

On the other side, twelve hundred customers press shoulder to shoulder beneath a vinyl banner that says GIVE THE GIFT OF WARMTH. Their breath clouds the glass. Their hands slap it. Their mouths open and close.

“Ten seconds,” Marcy says.

She is my manager. She has a whistle, a radio, and a strip of athletic tape wrapped around each wrist. She did not have the tape last year. Last year a grandmother dislocated both her thumbs over a SleekPack carry-on.

“Positions,” Marcy says.

I roll my neck. Check my laces. Check my utility belt.

Box cutter. Scanner. Gauze. Protein gel. Tourniquet. Two pens.

No employee discount card. Those get stolen.

Duo stands beside me in Men’s Performance Outerwear. First Black Friday. Twenty years old. Pretty good kid. He has gel in his hair and hope in his face.

Hope is bad protective equipment.

“Don’t let them surround you,” I tell him.

He nods.

“If they go down, don’t help unless they’re holding merchandise.”

He nods again.

“And don’t bleed on the face-outs.”

“Got it.”

He doesn’t got it.

The shoppers beyond the gate scream and hiss and claw and moan. The sound comes through the metal as one huge broken word.

Warmth.

Not just warmth. I hear the rest.

My daughter says everybody has one.

My husband left and this will show the boys Christmas is normal.

My boss wears PoleFace™.

My sister thinks I’m cheap.

If I come home without it, they will know what I am.

Most employees only hear noise. I hear the customers.

I have spoken Black Friday since my second one.

Marcy lifts her hand.

“Remember,” she says, “customer care starts with interpersonal cohesiveness.”

The gate rises.

Fingers appear underneath, pale and pink and bent like worms through a storm drain. Then arms. Heads. Teeth.

The first shopper crawls through before the gate reaches knee height. He is wearing a suit and one shoe. His cheek scrapes the floor. He leaves skin behind, but he has his coupon held between his front teeth.

“COAL,” he says. “COAL COAL COAL.”

Coalmeister insulated work coat. Black. Medium. He needs it because his father called him soft at Thanksgiving. His father is dead, but that does not make the opinion less active.

I pull the coat from the rack and swing it out of reach.

“Regular price two seventy-nine,” I say. “Black Friday Doorbreaker, one nineteen ninety-nine.”

“COAL!”

“Rewards members get another fifteen off.”

He stops.

The whole flood parts around him. Bodies hit tables. A woman climbs a mannequin and breaks its arm off. Someone goes down in Accessories. The noise changes around the body but does not slow.

The man in the suit fumbles for his phone.

“Would you like to enroll?” I ask.

He weeps.

That is sale one.

By 6:08 a.m. I have fourteen coats, six thermal systems, and three waterproof shells in committed hands. Duo has sold a scarf.

He is trying to reason with a woman who has a child carrier strapped to her chest. The carrier is empty.

“BLUE,” she says.

“There’s blue right there,” Duo says.

“BLUE!”

He grabs the first blue jacket he sees.

Wrong.

She bites him through the sleeve.

Duo screams. She shakes her head like a terrier. His arm flaps with it.

I get behind her and hook my forearm across her throat. She smells like cinnamon coffee and old sleep. I squeeze until her jaw opens. Duo falls backward into a cube of fleece pullovers.

“Midnight blue,” I tell him. “Not arctic blue.”

“How the hell would I know that?”

“Listen.”

“She’s just screaming.”

The woman lunges for his face.

I shove the correct jacket into her hands. PoleFace™ SuperShell Expedition, women’s petite large, midnight blue. Windproof membrane. Powder skirt. Seventeen-ounce recycled fill.

She goes still.

Her eyes clear for half a second.

“My baby girl,” she whispers.

There is no baby girl. There was one in March. Hospital bracelets in a kitchen drawer. Husband sleeping in the basement. She thinks the coat will make somebody come upstairs.

“Register seven,” I say.

She runs.

Duo looks at the bite. Four red half-moons through the fabric.

“Did she break skin?”

“No.”

Blood appears.

“Little bit,” he says.

“Bandage it. You’re on conversion.”

Marcy blows her whistle. Two short. One long.

Casualty in Home Goods. Code Beige. Facilities needs a path.

Christmas music plays over the speakers. Bells. Children. Snow.

It never snows inside the mall except for the foam they spray near Santa’s Village. Last year the foam covered three bodies until January inventory. One had a name badge from Pretzel Palace. The other two were customers and therefore somebody else’s numbers.

At 6:30, the first wave thins.

The floor is bright with wrappers, spit, blood, and crushed promotional cards. A shopping cart rests upside down on a display of moisture-wicking socks. A hand sticks from beneath it, still holding a twenty-percent coupon.

I check the hand.

Expired.

I move on.

My personal goal is thirty-eight thousand dollars.

Thirty-eight beats the district Black Friday record by nine hundred. It also wins the Peak Performer contest. Peak Performer gets a PoleFace™ AuroraMax parka, any in-stock size, retail value eleven hundred dollars.

My mother is a women’s medium.

She hasn’t owned a new winter coat since my father left. She wears his old canvas one, sleeves rolled twice, zipper missing three teeth. It smells like the garage where he used to smoke.

She got laid off from the dental lab in August. Downsizing. They sent her home with a mug that says THANK YOU FOR MAKING US SMILE.

She doesn’t drink coffee.

The AuroraMax is better than a job anyway. Nine hundred fill-power goose down. Welded seams. Heated collar. Internal rescue reflector. Lifetime warranty for defects in materials and workmanship.

A coat like that says a thing.

It says I remember you waiting in the car after my night shifts because the buses stopped running.

It says I know what the electric bill looks like.

It says I am not my father.

At 6:47, Marcy radios me.

“Daniel, status?”

“Thirteen four.”

“Thousand?”

“What else?”

She laughs once. Marcy likes me because I understand the mission.

“Corporate projects twenty-nine storewide fatalities,” she says. “We’re only at eleven. Strong safety performance.”

“Any in Outdoor?”

“Two nonresponsive. One uncertain.”

“Employees?”

“Customers.”

“Good.”

“Keep pushing attachments.”

I attach two pairs of SnowBlind gloves to a man whose left ear is hanging by skin. He wants a coat for his son. His son has not spoken to him in six months because the man borrowed money and bought a fishing boat.

“GLOVES,” he growls.

“You’ll want conductive fingertips,” I say. “Kids live on their phones.”

His face collapses with gratitude.

“BOY.”

“I know.”

I know all of them.

That is my advantage.

My first Black Friday, I think the noise is just noise. I am seasonal. Seventeen. One week of training and a red polo two sizes too big.

The gate opens and a woman knocks out my front tooth with a toaster oven.

I finish the shift.

My second Black Friday, a customer bites the web between my thumb and finger because I reach for the same last pair of lambskin driving gloves. His teeth go deep. His slobber hot.

The wound heals into a pale sickle. Half circle. My lucky Friday scar.

After that I understand.

Not speech exactly. Need.

Need has grammar. Shame is a verb. Love is usually an object.

My third Black Friday, I sell twenty-two thousand before lunch. A regional vice president watches me calm six frothing teachers with a single rack of discounted quilted vests.

My fourth, I become captain.

This is my fifth.

Five makes you permanent.

At 7:15, Duo comes back from First Aid with his arm wrapped.

He looks pale.

“You hear them yet?” I ask.

“Hear what?”

“You will.”

A teenage boy rushes us carrying three coats. One for his mother, one for his girlfriend, one for himself. He has no money for all three. He knows this. He has known it since parking.

“ONE,” he says. “ONE ONE ONE.”

Duo flinches.

“What’s he saying?” I ask.

“Nothing.”

The boy slams his forehead into a rack.

“He’s saying one,” Duo says.

“Under that.”

Duo stares.

The boy lifts his head. Blood sheets down his nose.

“Choose me,” Duo whispers.

There it is.

The boy’s mother works nights cleaning offices. His girlfriend says she may transfer schools. He thinks one coat can stop one woman from leaving. He cannot decide which woman.

I put the girlfriend’s coat back.

“Family first,” I say.

The boy snarls.

“Trust me.”

I sell him the men’s and the mother’s coat with a six-month deferred-interest plan. Two units. One attachment.

Duo watches him go.

“You just picked for him.”

“He needed leadership.”

“What if he wanted the other one?”

“Then he should’ve used clear language.”

At eight, we get the family packs.

Family packs are the worst.

Single customers are points. Families are geometry. Mothers protect children. Husbands protect discounts. Grandparents block aisles. Everybody has teeth.

A group of seven storms Performance Outerwear chanting, “MATCH MATCH MATCH.”

They want coordinated holiday photos. They have not taken a family photo in nine years because the oldest daughter married a man nobody likes. This year the man is gone. Matching coats mean restoration.

They need two men’s large, one men’s tall medium, three women’s assorted, one youth extra small.

We have six.

The grandmother sees that immediately.

“SEVEN,” she says.

“Six is still a strong visual statement,” I tell her.

“SEVEN.”

“The youth can layer.”

She comes over the display table.

I meet her with a folded SuperShell across both hands. She bites the collar, misses me, and gets eleven hundred-denier nylon between her teeth.

“Duo,” I say. “Inventory.”

He scans the tag while I hold the grandmother’s head back.

“Zero,” he says.

“Check alternate colors.”

“Zero.”

“Nearby stores.”

He checks.

The grandmother chews through the shell.

“Nothing.”

The family closes in.

Their eyes are wet. Foam ropes their lips. One of the men has somebody else’s fingernail stuck in his forehead.

“Substitute SleekPack alpine puffers,” I say. “Same silhouette. Better photo contrast.”

They hesitate.

“Forty percent lower price.”

Six heads turn.

The grandmother spits nylon.

“LOWER.”

“Plus free garment bags with six or more.”

They buy eight.

At 8:26, I cross twenty thousand.

Marcy shakes my hand while Facilities removes a body from under the register queue. The body is small. Youth size, maybe.

“Great numbers,” she says.

“Traffic is healthy.”

“Duo’s lagging.”

“He’ll convert.”

“He looks sick.”

“New language acquisition.”

Marcy nods. She was bitten in 2011 but never learned. Some people don’t have the ear.

She points to a smear on my chest.

“Is that yours?”

“No.”

“Outstanding.”

By ten, the food court opens.

The smell of fried dough and scorched cheese pushes into the store. It covers the blood smell without removing it. Like air freshener in a kennel.

Break is mandatory after five hours unless an active trampling event creates critical staffing needs. Marcy sends Duo and me together.

We step over a dead security guard near the escalator. His radio still says, “Maintain calm, maintain calm,” though his throat is open.

At the bottom, a woman sits beside a planter with a little girl in her lap.

The woman is not infected. Or not fully. She rocks back and forth.

The girl’s shoe is missing.

“Help,” the woman says.

Duo stops.

I keep walking.

“Daniel.”

“We’re on thirty minutes.”

The woman looks up. Her face is scratched raw.

“Somebody stepped on her.”

“Guest Services has incident forms.”

“She isn’t breathing.”

Duo kneels.

I look toward the food court. Lines at every counter. A man beats another man with a tray near Noodle Emperor. Normal capacity.

Duo puts his fingers against the girl’s neck.

“Call somebody,” he says.

“Security’s occupied.”

“Call an ambulance.”

“They stage across Route Nine until the rush ends.”

The woman makes a low animal sound. Not Black Friday. Older.

I hand her my protein gel.

Duo stares at me.

“What?”

“You gave her food.”

“She’ll crash.”

“The kid is dead.”

“Then the mother definitely needs calories.”

The woman tears open the gel with her teeth. Apple-cinnamon. Thirty grams of protein.

I buy a slice of pizza and a sports drink. Duo buys nothing.

He follows me to a table beneath a giant plastic wreath. The wreath says BELIEVE.

He sits but doesn’t look at me.

“You’re at twenty-three eight,” he says.

“Twenty-four one. Web pickup counts if I assist.”

“You care about that right now?”

“It’s Black Friday.”

“People are dead.”

“People die every year.”

“That makes it worse.”

“It makes it forecastable.”

He presses both hands to his face.

The bite dressing is soaked through.

“You should change that,” I tell him.

“I can hear them.”

I take a drink.

“Congratulations.”

“No. No, it’s—” He looks toward the escalator.

A man drags a television by its cord. Behind him, another man crawls after it, one ankle bent sideways.

“They don’t want this stuff,” Duo says. “Not really.”

“Some do.”

“They want people to love them.”

“Love has product categories.”

“That’s insane.”

“Jewelry, electronics, home fragrance.”

“You know what I mean.”

I do.

I fold my pizza slice and take a bite.

Duo says, “That woman in the blue coat. Her baby died.”

“March.”

“You knew?”

“She was pretty loud.”

“And you sold her the coat.”

“It was the correct size.”

“What happens when she gets home?”

“She owns a quality shell.”

He stands so fast the table jumps.

“You’re sick.”

“Employee health is on level three.”

“I mean you.”

Across the food court, someone screams over a coffee machine. The scream becomes a gurgle. The Christmas song changes.

Duo looks at my badge. DANIEL — CUSTOMER SOLUTIONS CAPTAIN.

“What are you trying to win?” he asks.

“AuroraMax.”

“That’s it?”

“Women’s medium.”

“For who?”

“My mother.”

He sits again.

The anger leaves his face. That bothers me more.

“She cold?” he asks.

“She needs a coat.”

“You could buy her one.”

“Not that one.”

“You’ve made twenty-four thousand dollars.”

“For the store.”

“Commission?”

“Seasonal incentive rate. Subject to adjustment.”

“So you can’t afford the coat you sell.”

“I can win it.”

Duo laughs. Not because it is funny.

I tell him about my mother. The dental lab. The mug. The old coat. The bus stop. I do not tell him about the night she sold her wedding ring to keep the heat on because that sounds manipulative.

“The parka proves it,” I say.

“Proves what?”

“That I can take care of her.”

“Does she think you don’t love her?”

“That’s not the point.”

“Does she?”

I wipe grease off my thumb.

Duo leans closer.

“The coat isn’t proof.”

“You’re new.”

“Your mother knows.”

“You haven’t met her.”

“She knows you care.”

“It has a lifetime warranty.”

He closes his eyes.

When he opens them, he pulls off his name badge and puts it on the table.

“I quit.”

“You need Marcy’s signature.”

“No, I don’t.”

“You’ll forfeit holiday differential.”

“Good.”

“You’ll be marked non-rehireable.”

“Great.”

He walks away.

At the escalator, he stops beside the woman and the little girl. He takes off his jacket and wraps it around the mother’s shoulders.

He looks back at me once.

I finish my pizza.

At 10:43, I return to the floor.

The store has had a recovery lull. Facilities stacks the nonresponsive customers in Juniors because Juniors is under renovation. The uncertain ones go near Housewares where there is an outlet.

Marcy catches me by Fragrance.

“Where’s Duo?”

“Career transition.”

“Damn it.”

“He wasn’t a fit.”

“We’re down six employees.”

“Seven. Hector’s in the wreath.”

She looks toward the atrium.

Two legs hang from the giant plastic greenery. Red shoes. Good visual merchandising.

“Can you cover North Face-Out and Performance?”

“I can cover all Outerwear.”

“That’s why you’re my guy.”

She taps my shoulder.

My mother used to do that before school. Two taps. Go be good.

I hit thirty thousand at noon.

Thirty-four at 12:38.

The final AuroraMax women’s medium hangs behind Customer Service in a clear security sleeve. White with silver trim. My mother hates white because it shows dirt, but this white has StainShield NanoBarrier™. Coffee, oil, salt, blood. Wipes clean.

I check it every ten minutes.

At 1:05, I sell a twelve-piece thermal bundle to a divorced father who believes base layers will convince his children that camping with him is safe.

At 1:12, a woman tears off part of my left sleeve when I tell her we do not stack military discount on Doorbreakers.

At 1:19, an elderly man dies standing up. The crowd holds him in place for six minutes. I use his shoulder as a display surface for knit caps.

At 1:31, I am at thirty-seven thousand, eight hundred and six dollars.

One good coat.

One average coat with gloves.

Four cheap scarves.

Marcy radios, “Daniel, south entrance incoming.”

The next wave hits before she finishes.

They pour from the mall corridor. Fifty. Eighty. More. Their shopping bags whip behind them. Their shoes slap tile. One woman carries a stroller over her head like a chair in a bar fight.

“OUTER,” they howl.

“COAT.”

“MEDIUM.”

“LAST.”

I climb the display platform.

“Welcome to Halloway Outfitters,” I shout. “I can help the next guest right here.”

They turn toward me.

That is the trick.

Do not fight the current. Price it.

I throw coats into hands. Call sizes. Recommend alternatives. Scan tags midair.

“Men’s tall large, charcoal!”

“Women’s petite small, plum!”

“Kids’ reversible, aisle four!”

“Waterproof is not water-resistant, sir!”

A man leaps for a SummitFurnace. I pivot, let him pass, and add matching snow pants before he hits the floor.

Thirty-seven nine.

Thirty-eight one.

The record.

I feel it like heat in my chest.

Marcy sees the number on her tablet. She blows her whistle and points at me.

Peak Performer.

My coat.

Then the crowd splits.

A woman comes through on all fours.

Her lips are blue. Her knees leave dark streaks. She wears a hospital scrub top under a fur vest. One hand clutches a store card. The other grips a torn size tag.

“WHITE,” she says.

I hear the rest.

Night shift. Double shift. Mother’s house. Two sons sleeping on a pullout couch. Heat shut off Wednesday. Younger boy asks if poor people still get Christmas. Older boy pretends not to listen.

Women’s medium.

AuroraMax.

White.

“No stock,” I say.

She shrieks.

Marcy steps between us.

“Ma’am, I’ll be happy to locate a comparable—”

The woman hits her.

Marcy goes down under a rack of packable vests. The woman lands on her chest and bites at her face.

Marcy blocks with both forearms.

“Daniel!”

I grab the woman’s hair.

She twists. Teeth snap an inch from my thumb scar.

“WHITE!”

“No stock.”

She kicks backward. Her heel catches my knee. I fall.

Marcy loses one strip of wrist tape. The woman’s teeth close around the soft part of her arm.

Marcy screams.

The crowd presses tighter. They smell violence and limited inventory.

Behind Customer Service, the AuroraMax gleams in its sleeve.

Women’s medium.

Peak Performer award. Subject to final verification.

My mother at the bus stop.

My mother’s rolled sleeves.

My mother holding the stupid smile mug.

The woman bites harder. Marcy’s blood runs down into her own armpit.

“Daniel!”

I can let the woman chew.

Managers are replaceable. The coat is not.

Duo’s voice comes back.

The coat isn’t proof.

That shit is sad.

I crawl behind the desk, rip the security sleeve open, and pull out the AuroraMax.

The fabric is light. Softer than anything should be at eleven hundred dollars.

“Ma’am,” I say.

The woman releases Marcy before I finish.

She turns.

Her face changes.

Not human. Then human. Then hungry again.

“WHITE.”

“Women’s AuroraMax, medium. StainShield. Rescue reflector. Rated to forty below.”

She reaches.

I hold it back.

“Store card?”

She slaps the card into my palm.

Even now, procedure matters.

I ring the coat at full price because the AuroraMax is excluded from Doorbreakers. She signs with a wet thumb. Approved.

I hand it over.

She presses it against her face.

For one second, she is only tired.

“My boys,” she says.

Then she runs.

Marcy lies under the rack, bleeding and laughing.

“You sold the prize,” she says.

“Full margin.”

“You idiot.”

“You’re welcome.”

Facilities arrives with gauze and a pallet jack. They lift Marcy onto the forks because the wheelchairs are all stolen.

She grabs my hand before they move her.

“You got the record,” she says.

“Does it count?”

“Corporate will love the story.”

The pallet jack squeaks away.

The floor settles.

Bodies in aisles. Coats gone. Racks bent. Christmas music skipping on the word joy.

I look through the front windows.

The woman in the white parka crosses the atrium. The coat is still unzipped. It balloons behind her. She looks almost winged.

Then the crowd swallows her.

My mother calls.

I watch the phone vibrate.

MOM.

Probably asking when I get off. Probably asking if I ate. Probably telling me not to drive if I’m too tired.

I let it ring twice.

Then three times.

I put the phone back in my pocket.

I have customers.

The announcement chimes overhead.

The Cartographer of Rain

In the city of Bellwether, rain did not fall at random.

It arrived by appointment.

Every morning, before the bakery ovens warmed and the tram bells began their quarrels, a narrow blue envelope appeared beneath the door of each household scheduled for rain. Inside was a card bearing the hour, the duration, and the particular character of the coming shower.

LIGHT DRIZZLE, 8:10–8:22 A.M.  
Suitable for gardens and mild regret.

HEAVY DOWNPOUR, 3:40–4:05 P.M.  
Secure washing lines. Avoid confessions.

MISTING RAIN, MIDNIGHT–DAWN.  
Dreams may feel unusually vivid.

No one knew who delivered the cards. Children sometimes waited awake beside their doors, but even when they kept their eyes fixed on the gap beneath the wood, they would blink and find the envelope already there.

The schedules were never wrong.

For seventy-three years, Bellwether’s rain had been planned by the Office of Atmospheric Order, a windowless building at the center of the city. Its director was rarely seen. Its workers wore gray coats and carried brass umbrellas, though none ever opened them.

Among those workers was a young cartographer named Elian Voss.

Elian did not draw maps of streets, rivers, or borders. He mapped rain.

Every day he sat in a long chamber beneath the Office, where hundreds of silver pipes descended from the ceiling. Each pipe ended in a glass valve marked with the name of a district: Marrow Square, Lantern Hill, the Old Botanical Quarter, Eastmarket, the harbor, the cemetery, and many others.

Across his desk lay a vast paper map of Bellwether. It was so detailed that every rooftop had its own tiny outline. Using blue ink, Elian marked where rain would fall and how it would travel.

His instructions came from above through a speaking tube.

“Rain over Lantern Hill at nine,” a voice would announce. “Seven minutes. Gentle.”

Elian would draw a pale blue circle around Lantern Hill, turn the appropriate valves, and watch a thread of water climb upward through the pipe.

The city’s weather followed his lines.

Elian had been taught never to improvise.

“Unscheduled rain causes disorder,” his supervisor, Madam Vale, often reminded him. “A wedding ruined. A roof unrepaired. A field overwatered. People think they want surprise, but surprise is merely suffering without notice.”

Madam Vale had worked at the Office for forty years. Her silver hair was pinned so tightly behind her head that Elian imagined it held all her thoughts in place.

He respected her. He feared her. He believed her.

Then, one Tuesday in late autumn, Elian found a cloud on his map.

It was no larger than a fingerprint.

At first he thought he had spilled ink. The little mark hovered above Wren Street, an ordinary lane of narrow houses near the river. But when he touched it, the cloud shifted away from his finger.

Elian stared.

Clouds did not appear on the maps. The Office created clouds only when and where they were needed, and those clouds existed outside, above the city—not as tiny moving shadows on paper.

He bent closer.

The cloud drifted along Wren Street, paused over Number Seventeen, and began to rain.

A patch of the map darkened.

At that exact moment, an alarm rang somewhere inside the Office.

Footsteps thundered overhead. Speaking tubes whistled. One of the silver pipes shuddered violently.

“Unauthorized precipitation,” cried a voice. “Wren Street!”

Elian covered the cloud with his hand just as Madam Vale entered the chamber.

She did not look frightened. Madam Vale never looked frightened. Yet one side of her collar was folded inward, which in her case amounted to panic.

“Did you open a valve?” she asked.

“No.”

“Did you alter the map?”

“No.”

Her eyes moved to his hand.

“What are you hiding?”

Elian hesitated.

Beneath his palm, something cool tickled his skin.

“Nothing,” he said.

Madam Vale studied him for a long moment. Then she crossed the room and inspected the valves. All were closed.

“Three minutes of rain,” she murmured. “No envelope. No warning.”

“Was anyone harmed?”

“That is not the point.”

She turned sharply and left. Within an hour, a team in gray coats had gone to Wren Street to interview witnesses, measure puddles, and confiscate any buckets of unauthorized water.

When Elian finally lifted his hand, the cloud was gone.

In its place, written in tiny blue letters, were two words:

FIND MIRA.

Elian had never heard the name.

That evening, instead of returning to his rented room above a tailor’s shop, he walked to Wren Street.

The lane was wet. Everywhere else in Bellwether, the stones were dry.

Residents stood in doorways discussing the event with the hushed excitement usually reserved for scandal or murder. A little girl knelt beside a puddle and touched it with both hands while her mother warned her that unclassified rain might be dirty.

Number Seventeen was an old house with green shutters. Elian knocked.

A woman opened the door.

She appeared to be about his age, with dark, unevenly cut hair and a yellow scarf. Her gaze dropped at once to the gray coat he had forgotten to remove.

“You’re from the Office,” she said.

“I need to ask about the rain.”

“So did the others. I told them I saw nothing.”

“Did you?”

She began to close the door.

“Elian,” he said quickly. “My name is Elian Voss.”

The door stopped.

The woman’s face changed. Not with recognition, exactly, but with the confirmation of something she had feared.

“You’d better come in,” she said.

Her name was Mira Sen.

The front room smelled of dust, tea, and damp wool. Jars lined every shelf. Each contained a little water, and each was labeled with a date.

“You collect rain,” Elian said.

“I collect memories.”

She took a jar from the mantelpiece. The label read: 14 MAY, YEAR 61—THUNDERSTORM, HARBOR DISTRICT.

“My father taught me,” she said. “Rain remembers where it has been.”

“That’s a superstition.”

“Is it?”

Mira unscrewed the lid and held the jar toward him.

At first Elian heard only the faint movement of water. Then came a distant sound: ropes creaking, gulls crying, a man laughing. He smelled salt and tar. For one impossible instant, he saw sunlight flashing between black storm clouds above the harbor.

He stepped back.

“What did you do?”

“Nothing. That rain fell on the day my father taught me to swim.”

She closed the jar, and the sounds vanished.

Elian stared at the rows of glass.

“The Office says rainwater loses all atmospheric properties after contact with the ground.”

“The Office says many things.”

“Why did the cloud tell me to find you?”

Mira looked toward the rain-streaked window.

“Because I asked it to.”

The answer was absurd enough that Elian laughed. When she did not, the sound died in his throat.

Mira led him upstairs to a small room beneath the roof. The ceiling had partially collapsed. Through a hole, Elian could see the night sky.

In the center of the room stood a battered copper basin. Above it floated the tiny cloud from his map.

It was the size of a loaf of bread now. It trembled as if exhausted.

“You stole an Office cloud,” Elian whispered.

“No. This one was never yours.”

Mira dipped two fingers into the basin and flicked droplets upward. The cloud absorbed them.

“My father called them wild clouds,” she said. “Before the Office, they crossed the country freely. They gathered over forests, rivers, fields, anywhere the wind carried them. They could rain for a minute or a week. They ruined picnics. They saved harvests. They made no appointments.”

“There are no wild clouds left.”

“There is one.”

Elian watched it curl around itself. The sight stirred a feeling he could not name. Pity, perhaps, though clouds were not supposed to be alive.

“How did it get here?”

“It has been hiding outside the city for years. The Office built weather towers along the walls to repel anything it does not control. But three days ago, the western tower failed for nine seconds.”

“And it came to you?”

“It came to this house. My father used to shelter them.”

Elian looked again at the jars.

“What happened to him?”

Mira’s expression hardened.

“The Office took him when I was ten.”

A silence followed.

Everyone in Bellwether had heard stories of people removed for atmospheric offenses: farmers who tampered with irrigation schedules, poets who released balloons during wind restrictions, old women who claimed their knees predicted storms more accurately than official notices. Most returned after fines and lectures.

Some did not.

“Why send the cloud to my map?” Elian asked.

Mira went to a desk and unfolded a brittle sheet of paper. It showed the city, but unlike Elian’s precise map, this one was covered in sweeping lines, curls, and spirals.

“My father drew this. He said the Office has a machine beneath the city—a reservoir where it stores the rain it takes from the sky.”

Elian had seen references to the Central Cistern in old maintenance manuals, but he had assumed it was merely a water tank.

Mira pointed to a spiral beneath the Office.

“The reservoir is almost full.”

“How could you know?”

“Listen.”

At first he heard the house settling. Then, from deep below the streets, came a low, continuous murmur.

Elian had always thought it was the underground trams.

“Water,” Mira said. “Millions of storms locked beneath Bellwether. Seventy-three years of rain.”

A chill moved through him.

“If the reservoir is full, the Office will drain it.”

“Where?”

“Usually excess water is sent into the eastern sea.”

“Usually?”

Elian remembered that morning’s instructions. Rainfall schedules had been reduced for months. Several valves were marked with red seals. Madam Vale had ordered new pressure gauges but refused to explain why.

Mira placed both hands on the desk.

“The sea is higher than it used to be. The eastern outlets are underwater. There is nowhere for the rain to go.”

“Then the engineers will find another solution.”

“They already have. My father warned them what would happen. That is why they took him.”

“What will happen?”

Mira looked up at the cloud.

“It will remember it was free.”

The next morning, Elian returned to work.

He told himself Mira was a liar. He told himself the sound under the streets was machinery and the cloud was some clever device. He told himself that an institution capable of scheduling every shower could certainly manage a reservoir.

Then he noticed the cracks in the floor.

They were thin, dark, and damp.

At noon, the speaking tube whistled.

“Elian Voss,” said Madam Vale’s voice. “Report to the Director’s chamber.”

No ordinary worker had met the Director. Some said he was ancient. Others believed the position had been empty for decades and the Office governed itself through recorded instructions.

Elian climbed seven flights of stairs.

The Director’s chamber occupied the top of the building. It had windows on every side, though all were covered by iron shutters. A man sat behind an enormous desk. He was small, bald, and surprisingly young.

Madam Vale stood beside him.

On the desk lay the tiny wild cloud, trapped inside a glass box.

“Elian,” the Director said pleasantly, “you visited Wren Street last night.”

Elian said nothing.

“You spoke with Mira Sen, daughter of Tomas Sen, formerly of this Office.”

“Formerly?”

“Her father was a gifted meteorologist. Unfortunately, he became sentimental.”

The Director tapped the box. The cloud flinched.

“He believed weather had desires. Rights, even. He released twelve clouds from the western station. The resulting storm killed three people.”

“Where is he now?”

“Dead.”

The word was delivered without cruelty, which made it crueler.

Madam Vale looked away.

The Director folded his hands.

“Miss Sen intends to breach the Central Cistern. She believes this will free the stored rain gradually. It will not. The pressure would destroy half the city.”

“Is the reservoir full?”

A pause.

“Nearly.”

“And the outlets?”

“Compromised.”

“What are you going to do?”

“Continue maintaining order.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

Madam Vale’s eyes widened. No one spoke to the Director that way.

Yet he only smiled.

“Order is always the answer, Mr. Voss.”

He opened a drawer and removed a blue card.

TORRENTIAL RAIN, ALL DISTRICTS, 6:00 P.M.  
Expected duration: Indefinite.

Elian read it twice.

“At six,” the Director said, “the reservoir walls will fail. We cannot prevent it. We can, however, preserve the principle upon which Bellwether was built.”

“You’re sending warning cards?”

“People will take shelter.”

“For how long?”

The Director did not answer.

Elian understood. The Office would call the disaster scheduled, and therefore controlled. Even as the city drowned, its officials would insist the rain had kept its appointment.

Something tapped against glass.

The wild cloud pressed itself to the side of the box nearest Elian. A single drop slid down the inside.

When it reached the desk, Elian heard a man laughing beside a harbor.

Memory.

He looked at Madam Vale.

She had heard it too.

“What did Tomas Sen tell you?” Elian asked her.

The Director’s smile vanished.

Madam Vale stood very still.

Then she said, “He told me the reservoir was never meant to hold rain forever.”

“Madam Vale,” the Director warned.

“He said rain changes when confined. It grows heavy with all the places it could not go.”

“Enough.”

“He said one day the city would have to choose between safety and control.”

The Director reached for a bell.

Madam Vale seized a brass umbrella from the stand and struck him across the hand. He cried out. Elian grabbed the glass box.

Together, he and Madam Vale ran.

They found Mira waiting in the map chamber.

“I assumed you would either help me or have me arrested,” she said. “I prefer this.”

The cracks in the floor were widening. Water shone below.

“We cannot breach the cistern,” Elian said. “The pressure will destroy the city.”

“And if we do nothing?”

“It destroys the city at six.”

Mira checked the clock. They had twenty-three minutes.

Madam Vale approached the great map.

“Tomas believed the rain could be released through the distribution pipes,” she said.

Elian shook his head. “The pipes are too narrow.”

“Individually.”

He looked at the hundreds of valves.

All his working life, he had opened them one district at a time, following careful schedules. Never more than twelve together. Never at full capacity.

“If we open every valve,” he said, “the rain will spread across the city.”

“The pressure may still rupture the pipes,” said Mira.

“Unless the rain chooses where to go.”

They looked at the cloud.

Elian broke the glass box with the handle of Madam Vale’s umbrella.

The cloud sprang upward. It circled the chamber once, shedding droplets, then hovered above the map.

“What now?” Mira asked.

Elian picked up his blue pen.

For years he had drawn circles, borders, and approved paths. He had believed precision was the same as wisdom.

Now he put the pen to the western edge of Bellwether and drew a single wandering line. It curved over rooftops, crossed the river, looped around the cemetery, spiraled through Marrow Square, and divided into a hundred tributaries. He gave it no destination.

The cloud followed.

Where it passed, the ink rose from the page in blue threads. The silver pipes began to hum.

“Open them,” Elian said.

He and Madam Vale ran along the walls, turning valves. Mira joined them.

One by one, district names lit up.

Lantern Hill. Eastmarket. Wren Street. The harbor. The gardens. The factories. The schools.

Pressure shook the room. Gauges cracked. Water burst from the floor in white jets.

Above them, bells rang across Bellwether as blue envelopes appeared beneath every door.

But the cards were blank.

At six o’clock, rain fell over the entire city.

It did not fall gently.

It hammered roofs, flooded gutters, tore leaves from trees, and turned streets into rivers. People shouted and ran for shelter. Bakers abandoned ovens. Trams stopped. Wedding guests crowded beneath tables. Children escaped their parents and danced barefoot in the squares.

Then the rain changed.

Over the hospital, it softened to a whisper.

Over the botanical gardens, it poured deep into the thirsty soil.

At the harbor, it blew sideways, driving boats safely toward shore.

Above old, weak roofs, it became mist.

It moved without lines or circles. It went where stone was hot, where roots were dry, where dusty windows waited to be washed. It avoided some streets altogether and drenched others for no reason anyone could determine.

The reservoir emptied.

All night, the wild cloud raced across Elian’s map, drawing its own design. Other clouds rose through the pipes to join it—small clouds, black clouds, silver clouds, clouds that smelled of pine forests, mountains, wheat fields, and distant seas.

They carried memories into the city.

In the rain, people heard forgotten songs. They smelled houses where they had lived as children. They remembered promises, faces, griefs they had buried, and joys they had misplaced.

Madam Vale stood beneath a broken pipe and wept, though later she insisted it was only water.

By dawn, the storm was over.

The Office of Atmospheric Order did not survive. Its foundations had cracked, its records had dissolved into blue pulp, and its Director was found on the roof clutching a stack of useless schedules.

Bellwether did survive.

There was damage, certainly. Cellars flooded. Chimneys fell. Marrow Square lost three statues, none widely mourned. But no one died.

In the weeks that followed, the city discovered how difficult it was to live without appointments.

Picnics were ruined. Washing got wet. Lovers quarreled in unexpected downpours. Farmers looked at the sky with suspicion. Citizens wrote furious letters demanding to know why weather had not been placed under the management of some responsible authority.

No one volunteered to rebuild the Office.

Madam Vale became keeper of the city archives. Mira opened a shop on Wren Street, where she sold empty jars and taught children how to listen to rain.

Elian continued making maps, though of a different kind.

He traveled beyond Bellwether, following storms through valleys and over hills. He mapped where rain wished to gather, where it lingered, where it refused to fall. His charts were inaccurate, changeable, and full of blank spaces.

They became very popular.

Years later, he returned to Wren Street during a summer shower.

Mira was sitting on the step outside Number Seventeen. Between them, the old copper basin had filled with rainwater.

“Was this scheduled?” Elian asked.

Mira tilted her face toward the clouds.

“No.”

“Do you think it means anything?”

“Probably not.”

They sat together in the rain.

Above Bellwether, clouds crossed the sky without permission, carrying the memories of oceans and rivers, rooftops and leaves. They promised nothing. They explained nothing.

And for the first time in many years, the city looked up.
